impacts.caseName: Teva Pharmaceuticals International GmbH v. Eli Lilly and Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the enablement requirement under 35 U.S.C. § 112 permits broad method claims reciting a genus of antibodies (anti-CGRP antagonist humanized monoclonal antibodies) for treating headache, where any member of the genus would be effective for the claimed treatment.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit denied en banc rehearing of a panel decision upholding Teva's broad method-of-treatment claims covering anti-CGRP antagonist antibodies for headache treatment, over a dissent arguing the claims are not enabled under Amgen v. Sanofi. The dissent contended the panel's holding undermines medical innovation by sustaining overly broad genus claims and creates confusion about enablement standards for method claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders with broad method-of-treatment claims covering a genus of biological compounds may find it easier to defend enablement challenges, particularly where the functional limitation (treatment efficacy) is inherently satisfied by membership in the claimed genus.
impacts.negativeImplications: Competitors and biosimilar developers face potentially broader blocking patents on therapeutic methods, as broad genus claims covering antibody-based treatments may survive enablement challenges even after the Supreme Court's tightening of enablement standards in Amgen v. Sanofi.

impacts.legalQuestion: Whether an exclusive license agreement conveyed 'all substantial rights' in the patents to the licensee such that the licensee could sue for infringement without joining the patent owner, and whether the agreement automatically terminated when the licensee shifted its business to patent enforcement.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed dismissal, holding that the exclusive license agreement between Texas A&M and TexasLDPC conveyed all substantial rights, making TexasLDPC effectively the patent owner entitled to sue alone. The court also held that TexasLDPC's shift to enforcement-only operations did not constitute cessation of business triggering automatic termination of the license.
impacts.positiveImplications: Exclusive licensees and patent assertion entities benefit from clarification that shifting business to enforcement activities does not necessarily terminate license agreements, and that broadly drafted exclusive licenses can confer standing to sue without joining the patent owner.
impacts.negativeImplications: Accused infringers lose a potential defense based on standing and joinder arguments, and technology companies face continued exposure to suits by exclusive licensees whose sole business is patent enforcement.

impacts.caseName: Versata Software, LLC v. Ford Motor Company
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court erred in excluding plaintiff's trade secret damages expert testimony and in overturning a jury's breach of contract damages award in a case involving misappropriation of automotive configuration software.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the trade secret damages judgment and remanded for a new trial, instructing the district court to reconsider two previously rejected damages models. The court also reversed the district court's post-trial reduction of the breach of contract jury award, reinstating the original jury verdict. The court affirmed liability for trade secret misappropriation under both the DTSA and Michigan law.
impacts.positiveImplications: Software licensors and trade secret holders benefit from the court's instruction to reconsider broader damages theories and the reinstatement of a jury's breach of contract award, reinforcing protections for proprietary software shared under license agreements.
impacts.negativeImplications: Companies that develop internal replacements for licensed software face significant exposure to trade secret misappropriation claims, and the remand for reconsideration of damages models could lead to substantially higher damages on retrial.

impacts.caseName: Constellation Designs, LLC v. LG Electronics Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims directed to non-uniform constellations for digital communication systems are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. § 101, and whether the district court properly denied JMOL on infringement and damages.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated the summary judgment of patent eligibility for certain claims of the '761 and '700 patents while affirming eligibility for claims of the '509 and '922 patents in a case involving communication systems using non-uniform constellations with increased capacity. The court affirmed the denial of JMOL on non-infringement and damages, preserving a willful infringement judgment against LG on the eligible claims.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in communications technology retain enforcement ability for sufficiently specific claims tied to concrete technical implementations, with the court affirming infringement and damages findings on eligible claims.
impacts.negativeImplications: Technology companies implementing industry-standard communication protocols face continued patent infringement exposure, though the partial vacatur on eligibility signals that broadly claimed mathematical optimization methods may still face § 101 challenges.

impacts.caseName: Cocona, Inc. v. VF Outdoor, LLC
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patent claims reciting a moisture vapor transmission rate (MVTR) range are indefinite when the specification identifies multiple testing methods that yield materially different results without specifying which method defines the claimed range.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's finding that asserted claims of the '287 patent directed to waterproof, breathable membrane materials are invalid as indefinite. The court held that specifying an MVTR range without adequately identifying which of multiple recognized testing methods applies fails to inform skilled artisans of the claim scope with reasonable certainty.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers in materials science and textile industries benefit from clarification that claims with quantitative performance ranges must adequately specify the measurement methodology, providing a strong indefiniteness defense.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders with claims reciting performance metrics measured by multiple standardized methods risk indefiniteness invalidation if the specification does not sufficiently specify the applicable testing protocol.

impacts.caseName: Satius Holding, LLC v. Samsung Electronics Co., Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether claims directed to a communications apparatus with a coupler matching transmitter impedance to the characteristic impedance of air are invalid for lack of enablement, even though the district court originally invalidated them on indefiniteness grounds.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit reversed the district court's indefiniteness ruling but affirmed the final judgment of invalidity on alternative enablement grounds. The court held that the asserted claims of the '385 patent fail to satisfy the enablement requirement because practicing the full scope of the claims would require undue experimentation.
impacts.positiveImplications: Defendants benefit from the court's willingness to affirm invalidity on alternative grounds not relied upon below, providing efficient resolution and demonstrating that appellate courts may reach enablement independently.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders face risk that even if they successfully challenge an indefiniteness ruling on appeal, the Federal Circuit may independently invalidate claims on enablement grounds, limiting the value of appealing invalidity judgments.

impacts.caseName: Exelixis, Inc. v. MSN Laboratories Private Ltd.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether patents claiming crystalline forms of cabozantinib (L)-malate salt satisfy the written description requirement of 35 U.S.C. § 112(a), where the specification discloses methods of preparation and characterization of the claimed salt forms.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit affirmed the district court's holding that Exelixis's Malate Salt Patents have adequate written description, upholding the validity of patents protecting the active pharmaceutical ingredient in Cabometyx® (cabozantinib) used to treat kidney, liver, and thyroid cancers. This preserves patent protection through 2030.
impacts.positiveImplications: Pharmaceutical innovators benefit from confirmation that patents claiming specific crystalline salt forms with detailed preparation methods and characterization data satisfy written description requirements, reinforcing patent protection for blockbuster cancer drugs.
impacts.negativeImplications: Generic pharmaceutical manufacturers like MSN face continued barriers to market entry for cabozantinib products, as the Federal Circuit's affirmance maintains Exelixis's patent exclusivity over the crystalline malate salt forms.

impacts.caseName: Epic Tech, LLC v. Pen-Tech Associates, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court provided sufficient reasoning when denying motions for Rule 11 sanctions and attorneys' fees under 35 U.S.C. § 285 in a case where the patent holder pursued infringement claims after related patent applications were rejected under § 101 and abandoned.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's denial of sanctions and fee-shifting motions, holding that the court's order provided insufficient detail for meaningful appellate review. The case involved a patent holder that filed suit despite multiple § 101 rejections of related applications and a sister court's invalidation of a related patent.
impacts.positiveImplications: Accused infringers seeking fee awards in exceptional cases benefit from the Federal Circuit's requirement that district courts provide detailed reasoning when denying fee motions, particularly where there are indicia of frivolous litigation such as prior § 101 rejections of related patents.
impacts.negativeImplications: Patent holders and their counsel face increased risk of fee-shifting when prosecuting infringement claims after related applications have been rejected on eligibility grounds, as appellate courts will scrutinize denials of fee motions more closely.

impacts.caseName: NCS Multistage Inc. v. Nine Energy Service, Inc.
impacts.legalQuestion: Whether the district court properly construed the term 'internal diameter' in patent claims directed to float tools used in oil and gas well casing operations, and what impact the construction has on infringement and validity determinations.
impacts.description: The Federal Circuit vacated and remanded the district court's judgment on infringement and validity of the '445 patent, which claims tools for positioning casing strings in oil and gas wellbores. The dispute centered on the construction of 'internal diameter' and its implications for both direct and induced infringement findings as well as damages.
impacts.positiveImplications: Patent holders in the oil and gas equipment industry may benefit from a more careful claim construction analysis on remand, potentially preserving infringement findings if the construction favors a broader reading.
impacts.negativeImplications: Equipment manufacturers face continued uncertainty regarding infringement liability in the energy services sector, as the remand reopens questions about claim scope and potential damages exposure.
